presidentialSuccession.name: Lenín Moreno
presidentialSuccession.notes: Elected with PAIS but broke with Correa; governed from the centre-right.

supremeCourt.name: Corte Nacional de Justicia (and Corte Constitucional)
supremeCourt.appointmentMethod: Judges selected through a merit competition run by the Judicial Council (Consejo de la Judicatura).
supremeCourt.fspEraChanges: A 2011 referendum under Correa restructured the judiciary, creating a transitional Judicial Council that overhauled judge selection; critics said it gave the executive undue influence over appointments, supporters cited reform of a dysfunctional system.
supremeCourt.stillServing: Post-Correa governments have continued to reshape the Judicial Council and the courts; the bench turns over through the merit-competition mechanism. Current members not itemized here.

courtHistory.event: Amid recurrent instability the older Corte Suprema was repeatedly reshaped across military and civilian governments.
President Gutiérrez and his congressional allies dissolved and re-packed the Supreme Court (the 'Pichi Corte') — the move triggered the 2005 crisis that ousted him.
Correa's new Constitution replaced the Corte Suprema with the Corte Nacional de Justicia and created the Corte Constitucional.

A referendum restructured the judiciary via a transitional Consejo de la Judicatura that overhauled judge selection — critics said it gave the executive undue influence; supporters cited reform of a dysfunctional system.
Post-Correa governments (Moreno, Lasso, Noboa) reshaped the Judicial Council and the bench again through merit competitions.

benchControl.note: The pre-Correa courts — including the 2004–05 Gutiérrez dissolution and re-packing crisis — were shaped by non-FSP governments; Correa first took office in January 2007.

Correa's 2008 Constitution replaced the Corte Suprema with the Corte Nacional de Justicia and a new Corte Constitucional; transition benches straddled the old and new systems, and the May 2011 referendum dissolved the old Judicial Council, giving the executive a direct role in its replacement (HRW).

Judges were appointed and removed by a Judicial Council composed almost entirely of former Correa-administration officials (HRW, 2014); the DPLF study by Luis Pásara documents executive sway over rulings. Supporters presented the overhaul as reform of a dysfunctional system.

After the February 2018 referendum under Moreno, a transitory citizen-participation council replaced the Correa-era Judicial Council and fully renewed the Constitutional Court (2019), which observers have since treated as an independent check (HRW, 2021); the correísta movement has been out of government throughout.

supremeCourt.justicesNote: Judges are selected by merit competition via the Consejo de la Judicatura; the bench turns over and is not itemized here.

fspParties.note: Ecuador's FSP member is Rafael Correa's movement — Alianza PAIS, now Revolución Ciudadana (UNES) — alongside smaller left parties. Important split: Correa's successor Lenín Moreno (2017–2021) broke with Correísmo and turned against it, which is why he is marked non-FSP even though he was elected on the PAIS ticket. Since 2017 the FSP-aligned bloc is Correísmo/RC, in opposition.

legislativeControl.seats: Before Correa, Ecuador had no FSP force in power; its traditional left was fragmented across a volatile party system.
Correa's Alianza PAIS won successive Assembly majorities, peaking at a two-thirds supermajority (100 of 137) in 2013.
The PAIS split: President Moreno broke with Correísmo, which reorganised as Revolución Ciudadana in opposition.

Correísmo (Revolución Ciudadana) has been the largest single bloc in the Assembly since 2021, without a majority and out of the presidency (Lasso, then Noboa). It stayed the largest bloc at the February 2025 election (67 of 151 to Noboa's ADN 66) but narrowed to a 66–66 tie after a pre-seating defection.

parties.name: PSC, Construye, local movements and a small left alliance

government.note: The 9 February 2025 election (CNE definitive results, 7 April 2025) returned a 151-seat Assembly — enlarged from 137 — with no majority. Correísmo's Revolución Ciudadana was again the largest single bloc (67) but stayed in opposition; President Noboa's ADN (66) governs as a minority, dependent on Pachakutik, the Social Christians and smaller movements. A pre-seating defection left RC and ADN level at 66 each. The non-government blocs do not form a common bloc. The small left alliance folded into 'others' includes the FSP-listed Partido Socialista Ecuatoriano, but it holds no seat in its own right.

parties.name: PSC, Pachakutik, local movements and independents

government.note: Snap election after President Lasso dissolved the Assembly ('muerte cruzada'); the new Assembly served only a truncated 2023–2025 term. Correísmo's Revolución Ciudadana was again the largest bloc (52 of 137) but stayed in opposition: Daniel Noboa won the presidency with ADN holding just 14 seats, governing through shifting pacts. Construye's presidential candidate Fernando Villavicencio was assassinated during the campaign. Bench sizes shifted slightly at seating as alliance members regrouped.

parties.name: Pachakutik, Izquierda Democrática, PSP, Fuerza Ecuador and local movements

government.note: PAIS kept an absolute majority (74 of 137, down from 100 in 2013) and Moreno won the presidency on its ticket — but within months he broke with Rafael Correa, and the Correísta wing (roughly 30 assembly members) split off into opposition. The majority elected here therefore stopped being FSP-aligned mid-term: from 2018 the FSP-aligned bloc was the Revolución Ciudadana rump in opposition, while Moreno's remaining PAIS governed from the centre-right with opposition votes.

parties.name: PSC, PSP, Pachakutik, Avanza and minor lists

government.note: Alianza PAIS held 100 of 137 seats — a two-thirds supermajority in its own right, enough to pass constitutional amendments without any other party.
